title: 2 Corinthians
aka: the second letter to the Corinthians
lead: Paul's most personal letter, written to a church he had hurt and been hurt by. It defends his ministry, explains why his plans changed, tells of his near-death in Asia and his meeting with Titus, asks for the collection for Jerusalem, and ends with a fierce defense against rivals he calls "super-apostles". Whether it is one letter or several joined together is a standing question.

sections.b: Paul founded the church in Corinth about AD 50 to 52 (Acts 18:1-18). He wrote to it at least twice before 2 Corinthians (1 Corinthians 5:9 and 1 Corinthians itself), made a short, painful visit (2 Corinthians 2:1), and wrote a letter "through many tears" (2 Corinthians 2:4) that Titus carried. After Titus brought good news in Macedonia (2 Corinthians 7:5-7), Paul wrote this letter and planned a third visit (2 Corinthians 12:14; 13:1-2), which Acts 20:2-3 places in the winter before he took the collection to Jerusalem. Dates differ by a year or two.
sections.refs: Acts 18:1-18; Acts 20:1-3; 1 Corinthians 5:9; 2 Corinthians 2:1-4; 2 Corinthians 7:5-7; 2 Corinthians 12:14; 2 Corinthians 13:1-2

sections.b: Paul's authorship of the letter is not disputed. Many scholars think it is made of two or more letters (for example 6:14-7:1 as a fragment, chapters 8 and 9 as two collection letters, chapters 10-13 as part of the tearful letter or as a later letter). Harris, Garland and Barnett defend the unity of the whole, with chapters 10-13 written after an interval; Thrall's commentary takes chapters 1-9 as one letter and 10-13 as a later, separate one. The Plain English Translation and the notes take no side but show where the seams are.
